source.title: Gaussian and non-Gaussian universality of data augmentation
source.authors: Kevin Han Huang; Peter Orbanz; Morgane Austern

record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes double-descent risk curves and reports that augmentation can shift their peaks, alter them through coordinate dependence, and produce triple descent in a sample-splitting setup. These results refine the conditions under which the curve appears.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own risk-curve results for ridgeless regression and related simple-network settings. The cited double-descent findings from other work are not recorded as rows. Universality bounds and results about estimator variance unrelated to double-descent risk curves are also left out.
record.test_reason: The study derives and simulates its own test-risk curves for ridgeless linear regression under data augmentation. The unaugmented curve shows a peak at d≈n followed by a second descent. Augmentation damps that peak and creates a new one at d≈nk. Positive ridge removes the spikes. Two-stage estimation gives triple descent. Peak location tracks an effective dimension set by covariance rank and augmentation structure. These results qualify V4, V5 and V6 in a non-deep model class. There are no deep-network size or epoch sweeps, and total sample size is never varied.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The paper's main contribution is universality results for augmented estimators: augmentation can increase or decrease variance, and may or may not regularize, depending on n, k, d and the estimator. On double descent, the authors conclude that augmentation regularizes near d≈n but leaves an unregularized spike near d≈nk for finite k, shifting the peak. They also find that sample splitting yields triple descent, and that peak location is governed by an effective dimension under coordinate dependence.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses theoretical random-matrix and universality analyses, with simulations, for augmented linear regression and simple linear-network settings; it does not reproduce the original deep-network size or epoch sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported risk curves change with augmentation count k, dimension-to-sample ratios, positive versus zero ridge regularization, sample-splitting allocation, and coordinate-dependence or covariance-rank structure.
record.problems: The key curve results are for ridgeless linear regression or closely related simple models, rather than deep networks. Several curve claims are supported by figures or qualitative descriptions without reported numerical uncertainty for the peak locations. The study does not sweep epochs or total sample size to test those versions.
record.rows_left_out: None of the study's own reported risk-curve outcomes bearing on the tested versions were left out. Cited results from other work, including prior double-descent findings, were excluded.

untested.parts: No deep-network model-size sweep; models are linear ridgeless regression and fixed-layer linear networks.
No sweep over epochs or training time.
Total training sample size is not varied near the threshold. Fig 7 only reallocates a fixed n between the two stages.
Effective dimension is tested only along the dimension axis d. Its prediction of peaks along the epoch or sample axes is not tested.
Label noise as the driver of the peak is not tested, and regularization is not optimally tuned.
There is no re-parameterization showing the second descent becomes a U-shaped curve.

missing.what: Peak positions under correlated versus isotropic noise injection on isotropic or correlated data: a peak at γ=2 instead of a regularization bump (case ii), and a peak at γ=2k in case (iv).
The pseudoinverse norm is unstable at γ=2(k−1), but the risk shows no peak there.
Peak positions are unaffected by whether labels use oracle or identity augmentation.

record.verdict_notes: Analysis is theoretical (random matrix theory and universality) with simulations at n=200 or n=100 and k=5; no deep networks. The study is not an original source for any version. The unaugmented double descent reproduces Hastie et al. (2022).

versions.untested_parts: No deep-network model-size sweep is reported; the principal peak analyses are for linear ridgeless regression.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
The study does not increase total training sample size near an interpolation threshold and measure whether test risk rises.
The reported curve analyses focus on ridgeless regression and related simple linear-network settings, not a broad survey of model classes.
The study discusses effective dimension for coordinate-dependence settings, but does not test one measure across model size, epochs, and sample size.

The study does not establish that label noise causes the peak or that regularization is optimally tuned. It does report effects of positive ridge regularization and multiple peaks in a sample-splitting setup.
No result shows that an appropriate effective parameter count turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: unaugmented oracle ridgeless regressor β̂₀^(ora)
rows.operation_detail: Sweep dimension d relative to sample size n and measure test risk.
rows.value: The unaugmented risk has a double-descent spike toward infinity around γ = 1.
rows.note: The paper identifies the unaugmented curve as exhibiting double descent; its own Figure 6 also includes an unaugmented curve.
rows.check: This is the study's own simulated and surrogate unaugmented curve (Figs 2, 6), not only a cited result, so it is usable as a control. The divergence at γ=1 reproduces Hastie et al.

rows.subject: oracle ridgeless regressor β̂₀^(ora)
rows.operation_detail: Sweep dimension d relative to n after adding independent noise to covariates.
rows.baseline: Unaugmented curve has a spike toward infinity around γ = 1.
rows.value: The augmented curve has a small local maximum around γ = 1 rather than the unaugmented spike.
rows.note: The authors describe this as a regularization effect around d ≈ n.
rows.check: The state is right. The spike at d≈n is replaced by a small local maximum, which the authors attribute to a regularization effect of noise injection. For V6 this is regularization damping the peak. For V4 it shows peak shape and location depend on augmentation.

rows.subject: oracle ridgeless regressor β̂₀^(ora)
rows.operation_detail: Sweep dimension d past the augmented sample-size scale.

conditions.value: d exceeds nk; γ exceeds k

rows.baseline: The augmented sample covariance is stable when d is below nk.
rows.value: The risk diverges when d asymptotically exceeds nk (γ exceeds k).
rows.note: The authors say the augmentation-induced instability occurs around d ≈ nk, shifting the risk spike from the unaugmented d ≈ n scale.
rows.check: The state should be observed, not partial. Fig 2's caption states a new double-descent peak appears at γ=5=k, with risk falling again afterwards. For V6, this row shows finite-k augmentation fails to regularize away the peak; it only relocates it.

source_check.locator_found: Section 6.1(ii) and closing discussion; Figure 2 caption; text lines 172–174, 1651–1655 and 1667–1669.

rows.subject: oracle ridge regressor β̂₀.₁^(ora)
rows.operation_detail: Sweep dimension d with positive ridge regularization.
rows.baseline: Ridgeless risk curves can have spikes.
rows.value: No risk spikes are observed for ridge regression with λ > 0.
rows.note: The study reports a positive ridge value, but does not claim it was optimally tuned.
rows.check: The ridge value is fixed at λ=0.1, not optimally tuned. 'No risk spikes' is a qualitative description based on Fig 6 (right).

rows.subject: two-stage ridgeless estimator β̂₀^(m)
rows.size_stated: dimension d varies; sample counts vary by split
rows.operation_detail: Sweep dimension d and vary the allocation of observations to the first-stage estimate and augmented estimator.
rows.baseline: The paper also plots the unaugmented estimator and the oracle estimator for comparison.
rows.value: Double-descent behavior for m = 0 and triple-descent behaviors for the sample-splitting estimates are described as clearly visible.
rows.note: This is an aggregate description of the separately plotted sample allocations; the authors attribute the additional spike to the first-stage estimator.
rows.check: The second peak comes from the first-stage regressor at d≈m, which is an artifact of the two-stage design. Per-allocation peak positions are not given numerically.

rows.subject: oracle ridgeless estimator β̂₀^(ora)
rows.operation_detail: Sweep dimension d under random permutations preserving coordinate partitions.
rows.baseline: The unaugmented peak depends on the effective dimension of the data.
rows.value: A peak is observed at γ = b, corresponding to d/b = n; the instability at γ = b(k − 1)/(b − 1) does not produce another risk peak.
rows.note: The authors describe an effective-dimension account involving coordinate dependence, and note that not every instability in the pseudoinverse creates a peak in risk.
rows.check: The peak appears at γ=b. The pseudoinverse instability at γ=b(k−1)/(b−1) produces no risk peak, so effective-dimension instability does not fully predict the peaks.

relationships.condition: Noise-injection augmentation near d≈n, and random-permutation augmentation
relationships.reason: The peak at d≈n shrinks to a small bump under augmentation (R2). Peak count and location depend on augmentation structure, with some instabilities producing no peak (R8).
relationships.display_finding: Augmentation reduced the d≈n peak to a small bump, while augmentation structure determined peak number and location, with some instabilities producing no peak.

source_check.reason: R2 shows damping at the original threshold, with the augmented peak relocated near d≈nk. R8 retains a risk peak at γ=b. V4 does not require an infinite spike or a peak at every spectral instability; these results preserve double descent.

relationships.condition: Cropping and sign-flipping with rank-deficient data covariance
relationships.reason: The unaugmented peak moves to d=2n (effective dimension d/2) while the augmented peak stays at d=kn, tracking effective dimension (R6, R7).
relationships.display_finding: The unaugmented peak shifted to d=2n with effective dimension d/2, while the augmented peak remained at d=kn.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Cropping and sign-flipping with rank-deficient data covariance
source_check.reason: R6 and R7 support effective-dimension predictions within the tested dimension sweeps: the unaugmented threshold is d/2=n and the augmented threshold is d=nk. A unified predictor across size, epochs and samples remains untested.

relationships.condition: Random permutations and correlated noise injection
relationships.reason: An effective-dimension instability at γ=b(k−1)/(b−1) gives no risk peak (R8). Per the text, Fig 12 shows the same for correlated noise at γ=2(k−1).
relationships.display_finding: Effective-dimension instabilities produced no risk peak at γ=b(k−1)/(b−1) for random permutations or at γ=2(k−1) for correlated noise.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Random permutations and correlated noise injection
source_check.reason: R8 and Appendix B.3.3.3 show that pseudoinverse instabilities at γ=b(k−1)/(b−1) and γ=2(k−1), respectively, produce no additional risk peak. Predicting peaks requires the risk-relevant matrix interaction, beyond identifying a spectral instability.

relationships.condition: Ridge λ=0.1, augmentation at d≈n, and the two-stage ridgeless estimator
relationships.reason: Positive ridge removes the spikes (R4). Augmentation-induced regularization damps the d≈n peak (R2). Two-stage estimation yields triple descent (R5).
relationships.display_finding: Ridge at λ=0.1 removed the spikes, augmentation damped the peak near d≈n, and two-stage ridgeless estimation produced triple descent.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Ridge λ=0.1, augmentation at d≈n, and the two-stage ridgeless estimator
source_check.reason: R2 and R4 establish peak damping and removal under the specified interventions; R5 establishes triple descent. These support the tested regularization and multiple-peak components, without establishing optimal tuning.

relationships.reason: Augmentation does not remove the peak; it relocates the divergence to d≈nk (R3).
relationships.display_finding: Finite augmentation shifted the divergence to d≈nk while leaving the peak intact.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: R3 establishes a surviving threshold divergence under finite augmentation with λ=0. It does not test disappearance under optimally tuned regularization, so it cannot establish the proposed limitation of that V6 component.
